newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila Hotel row sparks govt-judiciary clash.
newsitem.headline: Manila Hotel row sparks govt-judiciary clash.

text.p: A Supreme Court verdict blocking the sale of the historic Manila Hotel to a Malaysian firm has rocked the Philippine economic landscape and provoked President Fidel Ramos to openly criticise the court, analysts said on Sunday.

They said Ramos's attack on the Supreme Court, spurred by businessmen's anxieties over the future of his privatisation programme, marked the first time in memory that a president had publicly tangled with the country's highest court.

A nationalist bloc of legislators cheered the court's ruling but Filipino and foreign businesmen deplored the verdict. Analysts and newspapers slammed the court for interfering in what they said was purely a government matter.
"We stare judicial tyranny in the face," political analyst Alex Magno said. "An imperial judiciary has emerged."

Dismayed by the Manila Hotel ruling, the local chambers of commerce of the United States, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Europe warned in a joint statement that foreign investors "will go elsewhere unless the rules are clear".
"The high court's decision (sends) a scary message to all foreign investors," the Manila Times newspaper said.

Once an object of derision for being allegedly subservient to late president Ferdinand Marcos, the court last week reasserted the clout of the judiciary by overturning a government award in its privatisation programme, a key facet of the country's economic reforms.
Ramos accused the court on Saturday of jeopardising reforms for the sake of an economic theory which had outlived its time.
"I regret the Supreme Court has given the outmoded and failed economic theory of protectionism a new lease on life in this country," he said.
The court stirred the political storm when it stopped the government from selling the historic, 75-year-old hotel Manila Hotel to Renong Bhd and ordered it handed over to a local company.
The Malaysian firm had won the bidding but the court said the hotel was a national treasure and priority must be given to a local company in line with the "Filipino First policy".
"Marcos prostituted the Supreme Court during his time ... Ironically by maintaining our respect for it, we let it grow into a monster," Magno said.
The judiciary has traditionally occupied a central place in the U.S.-style presidential system in the Philippines, but some analysts have questioned the pervasive role it is beginning to play.

"In some Asian countries, people try to settle their disputes by conciliation and lawyers are looked down upon," human rights lawyer Rene Saguisag said. "But lawyers have dominated our culture, everything in this country, including politics."
The judiciary's emergence as a force to reckon with in government efforts to liberalise the economy contrasts sharply with its docile image when Marcos was in power.
With the courts backing his martial law decrees, Marcos ruled for 20 years until he was ousted by a popular revolt in 1986.
Besides the Manila Hotel ruling, a series of recent decisions by various courts have reinforced the perception of an "activist" judiciary, analysts said.

These include a ruling by an appeals court to temporarily halt the privatisation of the Manila waterworks system after the government had awarded the contracts to two consortiums jointly owned by Filipinos and foreigners.

Two other cases questioning major state economic programmes are pending in the Supreme Court. In one case, four congressmen are asking the court to strike down a law deregulating the oil industry on the grounds that it would spark rises in fuel prices. The law went into effect on Saturday.

In the other case, tribesmen have asked the court to declare void a new law allowing foreigners to own up to 100 percent equity in mining projects. They argue that natural resources are the nation's heritage.
